title: Simulating Lexical Semantic Change from Sense-Annotated Data
venue: EvoLang13 (The Evolution of Language: Proceedings of the 13th International Conference); arXiv 2001.03216

selection.evidence: Opened 2026-11-26 night (arena-lsc session) as the origin of the graded/binary JSD definitions used by DWUG and SemEval-2027 Task 3, to see how its own gold treats sampling noise (arena-lsc F37). Chosen before reading results.

cost.compute_notes: PDF read in full (12 pp; Table 4 from the page image). semcor_lsc.zip (1.6 MB) from IMS; null_check.py < 1 min CPU.

triggers: definition of graded and binary lexical semantic change
sense frequency distribution Jensen-Shannon distance gold
polysemy and frequency baselines for change detection
synthetic LSC by splitting sense-annotated corpus

claims.statement: Graded LSC of a word is G(w) = Jensen-Shannon distance between its sense frequency distributions in the two corpora; binary LSC B(w) = 1 if some sense has probability >= 0.1 in one corpus and 0 in the other.
claims.scope: Section 3.2. The definition the DWUG datasets and SemEval-2027 Task 3 Subtask 1b inherit (as cluster-JSD).

our_assessment.why: A definition, recomputed exactly from the deposit (max abs error 4.9e-11 over 148 lemmas). As a population quantity it is sound; applied to observed counts it is a plug-in estimate whose no-change expectation is far from 0 at these sizes (c3), which the definition does not mention. The paper names polysemy and frequency as confounds, not sample size.

claims.statement: On the 148-lemma SemCor-LSC testset, vector-space models reach graded Spearman mean .159, best .451 (SGNS+OP+CD); the polysemy baseline .349 and the frequency baseline .120; the best models outperform both baselines.
claims.scope: Table 4; best = maximum over many model x alignment x measure configurations, averaged over five runs.

our_assessment.why: Both baselines reproduced exactly from the deposited poly.tsv and freq.tsv (.349, .120). A third baseline the paper lacks, the no-change expectation of the plug-in distance (knows only each lemma's sense count K and the two sample sizes), reaches .422 (c3): above the mean model and the polysemy baseline, .03 below the best configuration, which is a maximum over many. The conclusion that the best models measure more than polysemy or frequency holds only against the two baselines reported.

claims.statement: Sampling noise in the SemCor-LSC gold: re-splitting each lemma's annotated uses at random between the halves (500 draws) gives a mean no-change distance of 0.151 against a mean gold of 0.314; 86/148 lemmas (58%) exceed their own null 95th percentile. The chi-square formula matches the permutation mean (Spearman .988, 8% low). Spearman(gold, formula) = .422, (gold, permutation mean) = .386; among the 62 lemmas not above their null, gold ranks like its null at .794.
claims.scope: Annotated uses per half: min 25, median 64. Which lemmas were deliberately changed (targets of step i) is not released, so changed here means above its own null.

our_assessment.why: Own measurement from the deposit; one synthetic set. A third of the testset carries no change distinguishable from re-splitting, and that part of the gold is ordered by K and n.

checked.how: unzip; testset/testset.tsv (lemma, T1, T2, freq1, freq2, freq_error, poly, freq, graded, binary), poly.tsv, freq.tsv
checked.result: graded recomputed from T1/T2 exactly; baselines .349/.120 reproduced

relations.why: Same research line; the later paper measures annotation robustness, this one defines the JSD gold; neither reports the plug-in no-change expectation.
Another graded gold whose ranking is partly set by K and n (here .42 from the noise formula alone).

open_questions: Which lemmas were step-(i) targets? With that list, does the noise formula still order the non-targets at ~.8, and how many non-targets exceed their null through sentence-level co-assignment with targets?
